Rule counts stay modest in these random hunts — minimal transversals are apparently not that numerous for random predicates (minimality + falsifiability constraints are restrictive). The engine handles whatever count arises within a bounded budget anyway.

Let me do one more push for a really large rules case, since it stresses both minimality-check throughput and serialization: exploit structure. Take K=1, one field x, domain [0..63] (U=64). Predicates p_i: x != i for i in 0..31 (32 preds). Train rows: values 0..31 (each once) → masks missing 1 bit each. Minimal hitting sets = pairs {i,j} — but falsifier requires window with x==i and x==j — impossible. Dead end again (disjoint falsesets).

Alternative: predicates p_i: x ≥ i... falsesets F_i = {x < i} nested. Rows x=a: mask = {i ≤ a}. Masks: prefixes. Minimal hitting sets of family of prefixes {0..a}: H hits {0..a} iff min(H) ≤ a ∀a∈train ⇔ min(H) ≤ a_min. Minimal: singletons {i}, i ≤ a_min. Few.

Key realization: many minimal hitting sets + falsifiers need falsesets overlapping in a rich way with rows outside those unions... To get C(32,4)-scale rule counts seems impossible; the number of minimal hitting sets of size ≤ 4 with each having a private row (≤10000 rows) — each rule of size k needs k private rows; rules sharing rows is possible. Max rules ≈ number of minimal transversals... I'll trust the bounded enumeration.

Actually, one more simple construction for MANY rules: family of masks where each mask is (all bits) minus one — can't falsify pairs. Family of masks that are large but with falsesets overlapping: F_i overlapping pairwise... e.g., preds over2 cells: p_i: (x != i) for i 0..7 on cell x AND preds q_j: (x != j) for j 8..15?? same cell again. Multi-cell: p_i^cell0: x != i (i 0..7), p^cell1... falsesets per cell disjoint within cell.

Use cmp with OR-like structure via sums? A comparison's falseset is some subset; two comparisons can have overlapping falsesets trivially: p: x+y !=3; q: x+y != 4 → falsesets {(1,2),(2,1),(0,3),(3,0)...} disjoint-ish values but overlapping WINDOWS? Falseset(p) = windows with sum 3; F(q) = sum 4 — disjoint. p: x+y ≥ 3, q: x*y... no products available. p: x+y ≥ 3 (F: sum ≤2), q: x ≥ 1 (F: x=0) → F(p) ∩ F(q) = {(0,0),(0,1),(0,2)} ✓ overlapping!

So thresholds give overlapping falsesets. Let me think: preds p_i: x ≥ i (i 0..7) and q_j: y ≥ j (j 0..7): F(p_i) = {x < i}, F(q_j) = {y < j}. Rows: masks of row (a,b) = {i ≤ a} ∪ {8+j ≤ b}... minimal hitting sets: H hits all rows iff min(H∩p) ≤ a_min over rows... singletons {p_i} with i ≤ min row x... plus combos: H = {p_i, q_j} hits iff (i ≤ a_min or...) — H hits row (a,b) iff (i ≤ a) or (j ≤ b) iff NOT (i > a AND j > b). For all rows (a,b) ∈ S: H hits iff for all (a,b)∈S: i ≤ a or j ≤ b. With rows = {(0,0),(7,7)}... take S = all (a,b) pairs: (a,b) = (i-1, j-1) exists → H fails. Take S = {(0,7),(7,0)}: H={p_0,q_0} trivially hits. Hmm.

H={p_i,q_j} minimal with falsifier: F(H) = {x<i, y<j} nonempty iff i≥1 and j≥1 ✓. Private of p_i: row with mask∩ H = {p_i}: row (a,b) with (i ≤ a) and NOT (j ≤ b) → b < j ≤ ... exists for rows with b ≤ j-1, a ≥ i. So with train rows covering enough grid, rules = {p_i, q_j} for all i,j with hitting condition on S... If S = ALL grid points (a,b), {p_i,q_j} fails at (i-1,j-1) → not hitting. Singletons {p_i}: fails at (i-1, b) if row exists → S all → fails. So no rules. If S = 64 rows restricted... 

The pattern: rules want SMALL train family; falsifiers want windows outside the rows' support. Take train rows = {(0,0)} only: mask = {} empty? Row (0,0) with p_i: x≥i → false for i≥1, p_0: x≥0 true. Mask = {p_0, q_0}. Minimal hitting sets of family {{p_0,q_0}} = {p_0}, {q_0} → 2 rules. Cond3: F(p_0) = {x<0} = ∅ → tautology → excluded!! p_0 = x ≥ 0 always true... 

Take train rows = {(3,3)} single row: mask = {p_0..p_3, q_0..q_3} (8 bits). Minimal hitting sets = 8 singletons. Falsifier of {p_i}: x < i nonempty iff i ≥ 1 → rules = {p_1},{p_2},{p_3},{q_1},{q_2},{q_3} = 6 rules. Meh.

Two rows {(3,0),(0,3)}: masks {p0-3,q0} and {p0,q0-3}: minimal hitting sets: {p0} (hits both ✓ minimal ✓), {q0}, {p1..p3 ∩ ...}: {p_i,q_j} i,j≥1: hits row1 via p_i ✓ row2 via q_j ✓ minimal ✓ falsifier x<i,y<j ✓ nonempty → rules = {p_1,q_1}... {p_3,q_3}: 9 rules + {p_0},{q_0} excluded (tautology: F(p_0)=x<0 empty) → 9 rules.

Generalize: rows = {(a,0),(0,a)} for a = 3: rule count 9. With predicates split x: p_i (i 0..15), y: q_j (j 0..15), rows = {(k,0),(0,k)} for k=3..: masks {p_0..p_3, q_0} and {p_0, q_0..q_3}: minimal hitting sets: singletons {p_0},{q_0} (tautologies, excluded); pairs {p_i,q_j} i,j ∈1..3 → 9. Still small.

To get ~C(32,4) we'd need maximal freedom in choosing 4 elements... The constraints (each element needs a private row/falsifier) make huge rule counts structurally implausible except in crafted cases with 10000 rows engineered as private providers. With N=10000 rows and 32 preds each row can serve as private for many elements... e.g., make all 32 preds pairwise-structured... 

Honestly: worst case is bounded by C(32,4)=35960 rules; even if reached, the engine does ≤ 41448 candidates × ~10µs + 36k rules × ~10µs + JSON ~4MB — ~1s. Output ≤ 64MiB cap: 36k rules × ~90B = 3.2MB ✓. So even the theoretical extreme is safe. I'm confident.
